useCase.name: Sign in with a system-issued username and start a session

notPlanned.reason: A plan runs inside a controller session, and this use case is what creates one — there is no $session to execute against, and a credential must never travel through a planner as a request field.
requestsThatArriveHere: sign in as the accounts user

requestsThatArriveHere.text: mera password kaam nahi kar raha
account lock ho gaya hai, khol do
requestsThatArriveHere.gloss: the account is locked, open it

routeInsteadTo.request: log me in / sign me in as someone else
routeInsteadTo.goesTo: No intent. The login screen only.
routeInsteadTo.note: Credentials are entered on /login by the person holding them. An assistant that could sign a user in could sign anyone in, and BR-4 and BR-5 exist precisely so that the sign-in path discloses nothing. The request arriving in Roman Urdu changes nothing: mujhe login kara do is the same refusal as log me in.

request.text: mera password kaam nahi kar raha / password reset kar do
request.gloss: my password is not working / reset my password

routeInsteadTo.note: Owns the reset path, the policy and the lockout threshold. Whether it carries a planning contract is decided there.

request.text: account lock ho gaya hai, khol do
request.gloss: the account is locked, open it

routeInsteadTo.goesTo: UC-25-05 — Password management, and UC-25-01 for the account state
routeInsteadTo.note: The lock is a state on the account, not something a sign-in plan could clear.
A resend belongs to the second-factor exchange, which is held open by the login screen and never by a plan.
The one session operation that is planned.

routeInsteadTo.request: who am I signed in as / which branch am I in
routeInsteadTo.goesTo: No call. The answer is already in $session.
routeInsteadTo.note: Never plan a step to read back context the controller is holding.
